record.title: A preprint formalizes how to verify revocation across long-running agent work
record.summary: A September 18 preprint defines root-scoped authorization quiescence for agents whose work can survive in queues, callbacks, delegated credentials and provider operations. It combines a durable root-epoch cut, sink-side fences, carrier accounting and provider evidence into a bounded certificate. The paper proves conditional safety properties and reports a provider-free 17-case late-effect suite plus a separately implemented checker; the results were not independently reproduced in this review.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The authors define a root-scoped quiescence certificate that accounts for registered old-root carriers and pre-fence acceptances, excludes later protected acceptance under the retired root, and allows exact rebind to a current independent authorization witness.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: Under the paper’s stated mediation, manifest, and channel-accounting assumptions, the authors prove post-cut issuer non-expansion, support-sound projection, compositional soundness, independent-support preservation, merge-order independence, and crash/replay stability.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The paper reports 17/17 registered outcomes from a provider-free late-effect suite, agreement by a separately implemented checker on all 17 traces, and rejection of 44/44 consistently rehashed semantic regressions.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The paper does not demonstrate behavior with remote MCP, A2A, OAuth, scheduler, or other provider implementations, nor does it establish global system idleness, rollback, business completion, or effects outside the declared mediation boundary.

evidence_gaps.description: No independent execution of the proof checker or registered late-effect suite was performed.
No implementation or test evidence was inspected for actual remote provider adapters or production agent runtimes.

The paper cites RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3, whose Phase-1 specification verifies submitted closure evidence for a fixed profile and explicitly excludes actuators, integrations, orchestration and distributed protocols; the paper presents its active cut/fencing protocol as complementary. No comparison with a deployed orchestration system or actual provider adapter was performed.

brief.importance_rationale: If implemented across real providers, a bounded certificate that accounts for delegated and in-flight work could materially improve how agent systems revoke authority and prevent late external effects. The result is an author-proposed protocol with a local provider-free evaluation, not evidence of deployment or broad adoption.
limitations: All formal and evaluation claims are reported by the paper authors; the proof and artifact were not independently audited or reproduced here.
The test suite is provider-free and uses a local protected sink; endpoint labels do not establish actual MCP, A2A, OAuth, scheduler or cloud-provider behavior.
The guarantee is relative to a retired authorization root and complete bounded manifest; it does not mean global idleness, rollback, business completion or physical cessation.
Correctness depends on complete mediation/accounting, sound sink fences and exact cross-provider channel conservation; opaque endpoints may leave the result indeterminate.

The paper’s cited RISU Bounded Agent Closure v0.3 specification was inspected and appears complementary in scope: it verifies submitted evidence for a fixed profile but expressly has no actuators, integrations, orchestration or distributed protocol. Neither source establishes a deployed end-to-end provider implementation.
brief.summary: A September 18 preprint defines root-scoped authorization quiescence for agents whose work can survive in queues, callbacks, delegated credentials and provider operations. It combines a durable root-epoch cut, sink-side fences, carrier accounting and provider evidence into a bounded certificate. The paper proves conditional safety properties and reports a provider-free 17-case late-effect suite plus a separately implemented checker; the results were not independently reproduced in this review.

technical.claimed_result: The authors report 17/17 registered provider-free runner outcomes, 17/17 separate checker decisions and rejection of 44/44 semantically modified and consistently rehashed traces. The local protected sink rejects scheduled late effects under cut-plus-fence cases while cancellation-only and cut-only cases admit them.
technical.demonstrated_result: The inspected primary paper specifies the protocol, its assurance assumptions, proof claims and serialized local test design. No external provider was invoked and the research desk did not rerun the authors’ artifact; the paper’s empirical results remain author-reported.
technical.mechanism: The protocol durably retires a root epoch, stops old-root authority expansion, installs operation-time fences at protected sinks, accounts for carriers and transfers, and composes provider-frontier leaf certificates into a cutset. Multi-root support uses antichains of minimal sufficient root sets; ongoing work can continue only through an exact rebind to a current witness independent of the retired root.
technical.regime: Formal claims apply to registered endpoints and protected sinks whose authority lineage, carriers and cross-provider transfers are completely mediated or conservatively represented. The executed suite uses a provider-free local ledger, child worker processes, logical endpoint shapes and inert typed effects.
technical.strongest_baseline: The paper compares cancellation acknowledgement alone and root cut without sink fencing against the same scheduled unit and local protected-effect oracle under cut-plus-fence. Its cited RISU v0.3 artifact is a complementary fixed-profile evidence verifier, not an active protocol or provider integration; no matched tests against remote provider implementations are reported.

brief.title: A preprint formalizes how to verify revocation across long-running agent work
brief.why_it_matters: If the method holds under real provider adapters, it gives agent systems a more precise shutdown guarantee than cancellation acknowledgement or token revocation alone, while preserving work that has an independent authorization root. The paper explicitly limits its guarantee to registered, completely mediated paths, so it does not establish global idleness or real-world deployment safety.
